options.text: A statute is automatically void whenever the judge would have written it differently on these facts.
options.misconception: confuses legality with a judge's preference

options.text: A long-standing trade custom overrides a clear statute because custom best expresses community values on these facts.

questions.explanation: Validity and moral worth are separate inquiries. A rule enacted through a recognized source binds even those who dislike it, and the remedy for a bad rule belongs in the lawmaking process rather than in a judge's private sense of fairness. Here the decisive point is the separation between legal validity and moral approval, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.

questions.stem: Suppose this: A merchant who refuses to honor a verbal promise is charged under an ordinance that was never publicly posted. No written rule defined the duty beforehand. Which choice identifies the principle that controls the outcome here?

options.text: Positivism holds that citizens must always obey every law regardless of its content or pedigree given the events just recounted.
options.misconception: misreads positivism as a duty to obey

options.text: Natural-law reasoning is available only to believers, so a secular judge cannot rely on it given the events just recounted.
options.misconception: assumes natural law needs a deity

options.text: Positivism separates law from morality at the point of identification, while natural-law theories treat moral correctness as part of what makes a rule truly law given the events just recounted.
Natural law denies any link between law and morality while positivism insists an immoral rule is never law given the events just recounted.

questions.explanation: The theories disagree about the criteria of legal validity, not about obedience. Positivism locates validity in social sources, while natural-law views build moral criteria into the concept of law itself. Here the decisive point is how positivism and natural-law theories differ, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Name each theory by where it locates the test of validity. Keep the inquiry on how positivism and natural-law theories differ.

options.text: A statute is automatically void whenever the judge would have written it differently on these facts.
options.misconception: confuses legality with a judge's preference

options.text: A long-standing trade custom overrides a clear statute because custom best expresses community values on these facts.

Here the decisive point is the separation between legal validity and moral approval, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Separate the question of whether a rule is valid from whether it is wise. Keep the inquiry on the separation between legal validity and moral approval.
